title: Hunger Warfare and a Fertilizer Crisis Are Straining Global Food Supplies | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: CFR's Michael Werz argues food is now a deliberate weapon of twenty-first-century warfare and maps a compounding crisis: Ukrainian grain exports running at a third of normal pace, a Hormuz-driven fertilizer squeeze that left phosphate structurally expensive while urea normalized, and a 90 percent chance of a very strong El Nino. The mechanical consequence is skipped phosphate application in 2026 and significant yield losses by 2028.

themes.theme: Food weaponization as standing military doctrine

insights.claim: Food weaponization has become an integral part of national security planning among mostly authoritarian states, and is being actively integrated into live conflicts rather than used only opportunistically.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: Treat agricultural chokepoints and grain infrastructure as recurring conflict targets when pricing ag commodity and shipping risk.
insights.quote: The use of food as a weapon of strategic warfare is a trend in military combat.
insights.locator: The use of food as a weapon of strategic warfare

insights.claim: Modern food weaponization differs from Leningrad or the Holodomor because control of global agricultural commodities and supply chains projects coercive influence far beyond the battlefield, notably Russia using wheat exports to deepen dependencies among African governments whose UN votes it needs.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: Grain export flows are a diplomatic instrument; watch Russian wheat pricing to African buyers as a leading indicator of bloc alignment at the UN.
insights.quote: Food weaponization now has transnational reach and geopolitical scope
insights.locator: What distinguishes this contemporary food weaponization strategy

insights.claim: Food weaponization operates through three overlapping strategies: manipulating food aid and supply routes, exploiting or manufacturing hunger to recruit fighters, and destroying production and distribution infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: A reusable taxonomy for screening conflict zones: which of the three modes is active tells you whether the shock hits logistics, labor, or long-run output.
insights.locator: Food weaponization has different dimensions

insights.claim: Ukraine's missile strikes on Russia's Novorossiysk grain export terminals mirrored Russia's own weaponization of food and undermined Ukraine's political standing with European supporters.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: Escalation is now two-sided in the Black Sea grain corridor, so freight and insurance risk premia apply to both Russian and Ukrainian export terminals.
insights.quote: Ukraine chose to undermine its strong political position among European supporters by mirroring Russia’s weaponization of food and ignoring international norms.
insights.locator: In late July, the Russian regime once again attacked

themes.theme: Black Sea output shock and freight economics

insights.claim: Over nine days in early August Ukraine exported 463,000 metric tons of grain, only about a third of the average pre-strike export pace of its Black Sea ports.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: A two-thirds collapse in Ukrainian export throughput is a direct bullish input to global wheat and corn balance sheets.
insights.quote: Over nine days in early August, Ukraine exported 463,000 metric tons (510,000 tons) of grain.
insights.locator: Squeezed at both ends: the input and output shocks

insights.claim: Most shipping companies suspended operations at Ukrainian ports after a missile struck a corn carrier in late July and killed ten sailors, meaning commercial shipping withdrawal, not physical port destruction, is the binding constraint on export volume.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: Watch war-risk insurance quotes and carrier willingness rather than terminal damage reports as the real-time gauge of Ukrainian export capacity.
insights.locator: Days before, most shipping companies had suspended operations

insights.claim: Overland alternatives to Ukrainian sea export cost $50 to $70 more per ton, and low water on the Danube has left that corridor unable to absorb meaningful volume.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: Quantifies the floor under landed grain costs for importers when the Black Sea route is disrupted; no cheap substitute exists.
insights.quote: alternative overland routes cost $50 to $70 dollars more per ton
insights.locator: This poses a real problem: alternative overland routes

insights.claim: Grain and crop prices have already repriced upward from January to July 2026: wheat up 24 percent, rice up 14 percent, soybeans up 8 percent, corn up 4 percent.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: Wheat is the clear relative leader of the agricultural complex in this shock, a spread worth noting versus corn.
insights.quote: wheat up 24 percent from January to July 2026, rice 14 percent, soybeans 8 percent, corn 4 percent
insights.locator: Several indicators are pointing to a more severe crisis in 2027

themes.theme: Fertilizer input shock: nitrogen versus phosphate divergence

insights.claim: The partial closure of the Strait of Hormuz caused by the Iran war has choked fertilizer flows, creating an input-side shock that compounds the Ukrainian output-side shock on the same grain balance.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: Dual-ended shocks compound rather than offset; model supply tightness at both planting and harvest stages, not just one.
insights.quote: These dual shocks are affecting global grain supplies at both ends of the production cycle simultaneously.
insights.locator: Current conflicts have the potential to create significant cumulative ripple effects

insights.claim: Urea prices rose 82 percent when the Iran war partially closed the Strait of Hormuz and then fell below pre-closure levels, because urea production is highly energy-intensive and tracks natural gas, which eased from its March European peak.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: Nitrogen fertilizer is effectively a levered gas trade; European TTF direction is the tell for urea pricing.
insights.quote: Urea, the most widely used nitrogen fertilizer in the world, saw its prices increase by 82 percent
insights.locator: Fertilizers that provide nitrogen and phosphate

insights.claim: Diammonium phosphate climbed steadily from $619 a ton in January to $781 in July 2026 and stayed elevated, because phosphate depends on mining and processing of phosphate rock rather than energy inputs and infrastructure underinvestment created structural supply constraints.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: Phosphate is the structurally short nutrient with no energy-price relief valve; favors phosphate producers over nitrogen producers on a multi-year view.
insights.quote: from $619 a ton in January to $781 in July
insights.locator: Meanwhile, diammonium phosphate (DAP)

insights.claim: The most important concentration of phosphate rock is in Morocco, which is why phosphate prices stayed elevated while nitrogen prices normalized.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: Geographic concentration of phosphate supply is a single-country dependency worth tracking for policy or export-control risk.
insights.locator: The structural shortage of phosphate availability

insights.claim: Nitrogen was up to 60 percent cheaper between April and July when measured against crop prices, a counterintuitive affordability that masks deeper vulnerabilities in the fertilizer complex.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: Cheap nitrogen relative to crops is a false all-clear; the binding constraint sits in phosphate, not nitrogen.
insights.quote: Nitrogen is up to 60 percent cheaper between April and July when measured against crop prices, but this is counterintuitive and masks deeper vulnerabilities.
insights.locator: Nitrogen is up to 60 percent cheaper

insights.claim: Farmers cut fertilizer purchases after the April 2026 price spike and the continued climb has not reversed those decisions, meaning demand destruction in fertilizer is already locked into the crop that follows.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: Fertilizer volume weakness now translates mechanically into lower yields later; a bearish fertilizer-volume, bullish-grain setup.
insights.quote: Farmers had already cut fertilizer purchases after the April price spike, and the continued climb has not reversed those decisions.
insights.locator: Several indicators are pointing to a more severe crisis in 2027

insights.claim: Northern Hemisphere and Brazilian growers make second-crop corn input purchase decisions between September and December, so the September-to-December 2026 buying window is when cheap urea and expensive phosphate will be locked in as a skewed nutrient mix.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: A dated decision window: September-December fertilizer order books are the observable leading indicator of 2027-28 yields.
insights.locator: For farmers, the climb in prices runs straight into the buying season

insights.claim: Soil phosphate reserves can absorb one season of skipped application but not two, producing a staged timeline in which 2027 yields hold or decline slightly and 2028 yields suffer significant losses from soil phosphate deficiency.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: A dated, mechanistic path to a 2028 grain supply shortfall that is largely already determined by 2026 purchasing behavior.
insights.quote: One season of skipping phosphate application can be absorbed by soil reserves; a second season of shortfall depletes those reserves, and yields fall in the third year.
insights.locator: This leaves phosphate underinvestment as the worrying legacy

insights.claim: Reduced nutrient availability caused by high fertilizer prices could further constrain Northern Hemisphere yields, pointing to a more severe food crisis in 2027 than in 2026.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: The crisis peak is forecast ahead, not behind; positioning based on 2026 price action may underprice 2027.
insights.locator: Several indicators are pointing to a more severe crisis in 2027

insights.claim: Current conflicts are expected to create significant cumulative ripple effects in the international food system over the next twelve to twenty-four months.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: Gives an explicit 12-24 month horizon for the food-inflation trade from the September 2026 baseline.
insights.locator: Current conflicts have the potential to create significant cumulative ripple effects

themes.theme: El Nino as the third, simultaneous shock

insights.claim: NOAA's Climate Prediction Center estimates a 90 percent chance of a very strong El Nino in the Pacific from November 2026 to January 2027, with high odds of it being the most significant such system since 1950.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: A near-certain, record-scale weather shock landing on top of already-tight grain and fertilizer balances.
insights.quote: a 90 percent chance of a very strong El Niño in the Pacific region from November 2026 to January 2027
insights.locator: Then there is the final shock

insights.claim: El Nino has historically driven Australian wheat yields 30.6 percent below trend, a pattern seen in ten of the last fifteen El Nino years since 1980.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: A quantified, high-hit-rate historical base rate for shorting Australian wheat supply into an El Nino winter.
insights.quote: El Niño has historically driven Australian wheat yields 30.6 percent below trend
insights.locator: Helios AI’s climate risk data through mid-August

insights.claim: Indian rice entering its reproductive stage faces extremely wet conditions on three-quarters of all days in the coming weeks, concentrated in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: Indian rice output risk feeds directly into export-restriction policy, historically a global rice price trigger.
insights.locator: Rice in India, with the crop moving into its reproductive stage

insights.claim: Brazil's soybean crop faces heat and drought potential for most days during the September planting window, followed by very wet conditions likely later in the reproductive stage.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: Two-sided weather risk on the largest soybean crop; a reason to expect elevated implied vol through the Brazilian season.
insights.locator: Brazil’s soybean crop, which has only just entered its growing cycle

insights.so_what: Names a specific commercial data source investors can track for crop-region climate risk.

themes.theme: Chokepoints and the new analytic stack for security planning

insights.claim: The Hormuz closure demonstrates that a single chokepoint can create global shocks within weeks, making chokepoint geopolitics a core risk variable rather than a tail scenario.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: Chokepoint disruption is fast-transmitting; positioning should assume weeks, not quarters, for price pass-through.
insights.quote: The Hormuz closure demonstrates that a single chokepoint can create global shocks within weeks.
insights.locator: The systematic and strategic incorporation of food security

insights.claim: National security assessments now require simultaneous analysis across chokepoint geopolitics, climate risk forecasting, commodity price volatility, fertilizer affordability, and long-term infrastructure investment.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: A checklist for building a multi-domain food-security risk model instead of siloed commodity analysis.
insights.quote: Welcome to the era of complex crisis scenarios.
insights.locator: Welcome to the era of complex crisis scenarios

insights.claim: Policymakers and military planners should treat agricultural supply-chain resilience with the urgency and strategic focus currently reserved for defense systems, implying a case for sustained public investment in food and fertilizer infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: If policy follows, agricultural logistics, storage and fertilizer capacity become a strategically funded category like defense.
insights.quote: Food supply chains require the same strategic investment and resilience planning as military systems.
insights.locator: Who will protect the world’s food systems?

insights.claim: Fertilizer and food prices have remained elevated in local currencies since the war began, meaning importing countries face a worse affordability picture than dollar-denominated price charts suggest.
insights.speaker: Michael Werz
insights.so_what: FX depreciation amplifies food inflation in import-dependent EMs; a channel for social and sovereign stress beyond headline commodity prices.
insights.locator: Fertilizer and food prices have remained elevated since the war began
